newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clouds of confetti greet Clinton in Tlaxcala.
newsitem.headline: Clouds of confetti greet Clinton in Tlaxcala.

text.p: President Bill Clinton escaped from the confines of closed meeting rooms to play tourist on Wednesday and the people of Tlaxcala welcomed him by tossing clouds of confetti into the air.
"Buenos Dias, Tlaxcala," Clinton said to cheering Mexicans who turned out in the town square to see him and Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo.

Thousands of peasants, given baseball caps and packed lunches, were bussed in by the government to see their first visiting foreign president and they waved Mexican and U.S. flags as Clinton swept into this colonial city 75 miles (120 km) east of Mexico City for his first encounter with "ordinary" Mexicans.
Referring to their packed lunch of a sandwich, two oranges and a fruit juice, one of the peasants quipped "This is Clinton: we ought to be eating McDonald's (hamburgers)."

Clinton is often envious of the freedom to see the countryside that his wife Hillary enjoys on her solo foreign travels, complaining that he is always cooped up in meetings handling affairs of state and does not have as much fun as she does.

So he spent the last day of his three-day visit to Mexico out of the capital, travelling by helicopter to this 500-year- old town. Later he was to visit the nearby spectacular pyramids of Teotihuacan.
Soon after his helicopter landed on a soccer field, Clinton was in a motorcade that drove a mile (1.6 km) through Tlaxcala.

Thousands of people lined the street, and from the balconies of buildings above, Mexicans tossed bags of red, white, green and blue confetti. The squares of paper coated the street and sprinkled onto the vehicles. People sang songs played by mariachi bands spaced throughout.

The entourage stopped at the town square and Clinton, still on crutches from a March 14 knee injury, climbed a podium situated in front of the 16th century palace housing the Tlaxcala state capital. With him was Mrs. Clinton, Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo and his wife, Nilda Patricia.
"President Clinton is a good friend of the Mexicans because he respects them," Zedillo told the crowd.
"And I'm sure that after these days in our country, he now knows us better. He now understands what he's known for a long time, that we Mexicans are a proud people," Zedillo added.
Clinton said that after the official work he and Zedillo had been doing in Mexico City, "Now we have come just to celebrate Mexico's people and culture with you."
He mentioned that he and Mrs. Clinton had honeymooned in Acapulco.

"It is an especially important day for my wife and for me because we were married about 22 years ago and we came to Mexico on our honeymoon. So we always love to come back, and this is a very romantic setting to be in today and we thank you for that," he said.
The crowd cheered when this was translated into Spanish for them.
Just like he was at a campaign event back home, Clinton shook hands from the enthusiastic crowd along the ropeline after his speech as a mariachi band played, "Viva Mexico."

Later, Clinton donned a cowboy hat and sat in the sun to watch a colourful dance performance. Traditional dancers wore headdresses festooned with brightly coloured feathers. Mexicans wearing sombreros pounded drums.
Clinton sang along when a group of children dressed in red costumes sang the traditional love song, "Cielito Lindo." He later joined them on stage and swayed and clapped his hands to the music.
